prompt: Each consumer has used a product and compared it with what they expected. Name the outcome the disconfirmation model predicts.

cases.text: From the booking photos, Lena expected an ordinary hotel room. She is given a room with a sea view and a free breakfast.
cases.explanation: Performance exceeded her expectations, so she is satisfied or even delighted.

cases.text: Omar's new running shoes feel exactly as comfortable as the reviews said they would.
cases.explanation: Performance matched his expectations, so he is satisfied.

cases.text: An ad promised a blender that crushes ice in seconds. At home, it struggles with soft fruit.
cases.explanation: Performance fell below the expectations the ad created, so the consumer is dissatisfied.

cases.text: Mei bought a budget phone expecting a basic camera. Its photos turn out as sharp as her friend's far more expensive phone.
cases.explanation: Performance exceeded what she expected from a budget phone.

cases.text: Ken orders his usual coffee at the café near work. It tastes the way it always does, which is what he expected.
cases.explanation: Performance matched his expectations: confirmation, and he is satisfied.

cases.text: A streaming service advertised thousands of new films. After signing up, Ana finds only a handful she has not already seen.
cases.explanation: The advertising raised her expectations, and performance fell below them.

question_text: Which of these purchases is most likely to leave the buyer with postpurchase dissonance?
hint: Think about the price, the importance of the decision, whether it can be undone, and what the rejected options offered.
correct_answer_citation: Week 09 · Cognitive Dissonance and Buyer's Regret

options.option_text: A $2 bottle of water bought at a kiosk on a hot day
options.option_explanation: The purchase is cheap, unimportant and easy to repeat, so there is little to doubt.

options.option_text: A $1,800 sofa sold as final sale, chosen over a cheaper model with washable covers that the chosen sofa lacks
options.option_explanation: Correct. It is expensive, important and hard to reverse, and the rejected sofa had an attractive feature the chosen one lacks.

options.option_text: The pack of gum the shopper buys every week at the checkout
options.option_explanation: A cheap, routine purchase gives the buyer little reason to doubt the choice.

options.option_text: A $40 sweater that can be returned within 30 days for a full refund
options.option_explanation: The purchase is modest and easy to reverse, which keeps dissonance low.

prompt: Each card describes something that reduces doubt after a purchase. Is the consumer reducing the dissonance on their own, or is the marketer helping?

cards.text: After buying a laptop, Ravi reads only articles that praise the model he chose.
cards.explanation: He seeks information that supports his choice.

cards.text: Jo scrolls past every ad for the camera she decided not to buy.
cards.explanation: She avoids information that favors the rejected option.

cards.text: Sam tells himself that the heated seats his new car lacks were never that important.
cards.explanation: He lowers the importance of the missing feature.

cards.text: A furniture store emails each buyer a thank-you note that lists what their new chair does well.
cards.explanation: A follow-up message thanks the customer and confirms the product's benefits.

cards.text: An airline lets customers change or cancel a booking free of charge for 24 hours after buying.
cards.explanation: An easy return policy reduces the risk the consumer feels after buying.

cards.text: A phone brand runs ads of happy owners filming their holidays with the phone.
cards.explanation: Advertising that shows satisfied owners reassures recent buyers as well as future ones.

cards.text: A support team answers a complaint about a faulty kettle within ten minutes and ships a replacement.
cards.explanation: Quick customer service keeps doubt from turning into dissatisfaction.

prompt: What is each consumer doing with a product? Sort the cards into the three disposal options.

cards.text: Nadia still rides her ten-year-old bicycle to work every day.
cards.explanation: She keeps it and uses it for its original purpose.

cards.text: Paul cuts his worn-out T-shirts into cleaning rags.
cards.explanation: He keeps them and finds a new use for them.

cards.text: Ali packs the family tent into the garage until next summer.
cards.explanation: He keeps it by storing it.

cards.text: Ruth lends her power drill to a neighbour for the weekend.
cards.explanation: Lending gets rid of the drill only for a while; it comes back.

cards.text: Theo rents out his camera for a week through a peer-to-peer rental site.
cards.explanation: Renting it out is a temporary way to part with the product.

cards.text: Ines throws her broken umbrella into the bin.
cards.explanation: Throwing it away gets rid of it for good.

cards.text: Marco gives his son's outgrown clothes to a cousin.
cards.explanation: Giving them away is a permanent disposal, and it is also lateral cycling.

cards.text: Yuki trades her old games console at a store for credit toward a new one.
cards.explanation: Trading it parts with the console for good.

cards.text: Sara sells her old phone to a stranger through a resale app.
cards.explanation: Selling it is permanent, and the phone passes to another consumer through lateral cycling.

question_text: An online retailer wants more first-time reviewers to write a review, and it has a budget for rewards. Based on the studies on the slide, which review request fits that goal best?
hint: Two findings matter here: who responds most to rewards paid only for helpful reviews, and what a message about helping the company does to the number of customers who write.
correct_answer_citation: Week 09 · Online Reviews as Postpurchase Behavior (Wadi et al., 2026b)

options.option_text: Pay a reward for any review, and ask customers to help the company
options.option_explanation: With a financial incentive, asking customers to help the company worked less well than asking them to help other shoppers.

options.option_text: Pay the reward only when the review is voted helpful, and ask customers to help the company
options.option_explanation: A reciprocal message led to longer reviews, but fewer customers chose to write one.

options.option_text: Pay the reward only when the review is voted helpful, and ask customers to help other shoppers
options.option_explanation: Correct. Helpful-only rewards raised review writing most among first-time reviewers, and the social-exchange message avoids the drop in writers that a reciprocal message causes.

options.option_text: Send the same request to everyone, because rewards affect first-time and experienced reviewers equally
options.option_explanation: The rewards raised writing and length more among first-time reviewers than among experienced ones.

prompt: Each consumer has a relationship with a brand. Name the type of loyalty, using repeat purchase and attitude.

cases.text: Dana buys the same toothpaste every month because it is the brand the corner shop stocks. She has no strong feelings about it.
cases.explanation: Repeat purchase without a strong attitude, driven by convenience.

cases.text: Luis loves a luxury watch brand and follows it online, but he has never been able to afford one of its watches.
cases.explanation: A strong positive attitude without repeat purchase, held back by price.

cases.text: Grace has flown the same airline for years and recommends it to everyone because she trusts it.
cases.explanation: Frequent repeat purchase combined with a strong positive attitude.

cases.text: Tom reorders the same brand of printer ink only because his printer accepts no other cartridge.
cases.explanation: Repeat purchase that comes from a lack of alternatives, not from attitude.

cases.text: Aiko adores a bakery across town but visits it only once a year because it is so far away.
cases.explanation: A strong attitude without repeat purchase, held back by availability.

cases.text: Ben buys his favourite running brand every season and would not consider another.
cases.explanation: He buys it again and again and holds a strong positive attitude toward it.

prompt: Each card is an instruction a consumer gives an AI agent to reorder a routine product. Does the instruction show loyalty to the brand, or reliance on the agent?

cards.text: "Reorder the same dog food brand I bought last month."
cards.explanation: The consumer names the brand, so the agent keeps it.

cards.text: "Buy the cheapest unscented cat litter you can find."
cards.explanation: Only a goal is stated, so the agent chooses the brand.

cards.text: "Get me two more boxes of my usual green tea."
cards.explanation: "My usual" names the brand the consumer already buys.

cards.text: "Find dishwasher tablets with the lowest price per wash."
cards.explanation: The instruction states a criterion and leaves the brand to the agent.

cards.text: "Order paper towels; pick whichever has the best reviews."
cards.explanation: The agent's choice depends on the goal it was given and the information it gathers.

cards.text: "Order the shampoo I always buy, in the large bottle."
cards.explanation: The consumer names the brand in the instruction, so the brand is secure.
